terms.gloss: a Roman mile, a thousand paces
evidence: Plin. Ep. 3.1.4: ambulat mīlia passuum tria
Traupman 60, 345: duo mīlia passuum, two miles
terms.comment: A thousand paces of five Roman feet: about 1,480 metres, some 1,618 yards against the 1,760 of the English mile, so a little under a tenth shorter (Lewis & Short s.v. mīlle; passus of five feet, Plin. NH 2.85). Also mīlle passūs, and often mīlle or mīlia alone: iterum ambulat mīlle (Plin. Ep. 3.1.7). Our word comes from mīlia.

evidence: Cic. Brut. 54: ad tertium mīliārium, at the third milestone
terms.comment: The stone set at every Roman mile; in Suetonius the mile itself (Lewis & Short), and so in Mercator, Thunberg and Pallas (Morgan–Owens). Also spelled mīlliārium.

phrases.latin: Māne lectulō continētur, hōrā secundā calceōs poscit, ambulat mīlia passuum tria nec minus animum quam corpus exercet.
phrases.english: In the morning he keeps to his bed; at the second hour he calls for his shoes and walks three miles, exercising his mind no less than his body.

phrases.latin: Perāctīs septem mīlibus passuum iterum ambulat mīlle
phrases.english: When he has done seven miles, he walks another mile

sources: Lewis & Short: mille · Lewis & Short: passus · Lewis & Short: miliarius
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. US length: mile.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 60, 345.
